Should the cache be the only copy of anything?
outline: Keys are placed with consistent hashing using many virtual nodes per server (or fixed hash slots as in Redis Cluster), and clients or a thin proxy keep the slot map so each request goes straight to the right node. Each primary has one or two replicas; a cluster manager detects failure through heartbeats and promotes a replica, then updates the slot map. Adding a node moves only some slots, and they move gradually to avoid a sudden miss storm. For hot keys, clients keep a tiny local cache for a second or two, or the key is copied under several suffixes and reads are spread across them. To prevent stampedes, use request coalescing or locks so only one caller rebuilds a missing value, add random jitter to TTLs, and refresh popular keys early. The cache is never the source of truth. The trade-off is memory cost versus database load.

title: Design a maps routing and ETA service
prompt: Design the routing part of a maps app: given a start and an end, return the fastest driving route and an accurate arrival time in under 300 ms, using live traffic. Assume a road graph of 500 million edges worldwide and 50,000 route requests/sec.
thinkAbout: Why is plain Dijkstra too slow on a planet-sized graph?
How can precomputing shortcuts make queries much faster?
How do you include live traffic without redoing all the precomputation?
How do you split the graph across machines?
Beyond the route's total time, what makes an ETA accurate?
outline: Store the road network as a graph where nodes are intersections and edges are road segments with base travel times. Because Dijkstra or A* over 500 million edges is too slow, precompute speed-ups: contraction hierarchies add shortcut edges so a query only explores a small part of the graph, and customizable variants (such as CRP) split the graph into cells whose internal shortcuts can be recomputed in seconds when traffic changes. Live speeds from phones and partners flow through a streaming pipeline that map-matches GPS points to road segments and updates edge weights every minute or so. Routing servers keep the graph for a region in memory, and cross-region trips combine results across boundaries. An ML model then adjusts the ETA using time of day, history and events. The trade-off is precomputation speed versus how fast traffic changes show up.

title: Design a real-time fraud detection system
prompt: Design a system that scores every card payment for fraud before it is approved, within 100 ms, for a payment company handling 20,000 transactions/sec. It should use recent behavior (for example 5 purchases in 2 minutes) and let analysts update rules without deploying code.
thinkAbout: Which signals can you compute ahead of time, and which must be computed live?
How do you count "transactions by this card in the last 10 minutes" quickly?
How do rules and an ML model work together in one decision?
What should happen if the scoring service is slow or down?
How do confirmed fraud reports flow back to improve the model?
outline: The payment service calls a scoring API synchronously with the transaction. The API reads features from an online feature store (such as Redis or another low-latency store): slow-changing ones like account age and usual countries are computed in batch, and fast ones like counts and amounts per card or device over 1, 10 and 60 minute windows are kept up to date by a stream processor reading every transaction from Kafka. The scorer runs a rules engine (analyst-editable rules stored as config) and an ML model, combining them into approve, review or decline. Strict timeouts apply, and if scoring is late, a fallback rule set decides so payments are never blocked by an outage. Every decision and its features are logged; chargebacks and analyst reviews become labels for retraining offline, using the same feature definitions. The trade-off is catching more fraud versus blocking good customers.

title: Design a distributed file system like GFS/HDFS
prompt: Design a file system that stores petabytes of very large files (many GB each) across thousands of cheap machines, built for big batch jobs that read and append in large chunks. Machines fail every day, and no data may be lost.
thinkAbout: Why use large chunks (for example 64 to 128 MB) instead of small blocks?
What does the metadata server store, and how do you keep it from becoming a bottleneck?
How do you notice a dead machine and restore the missing copies?
Where should you place the 3 copies of a chunk?
How do you keep the metadata server itself from being a single point of failure?
outline: Files are split into large chunks (for example 128 MB), and each chunk is stored as a normal file on 3 chunk servers. A metadata server (master) keeps the namespace, the file-to-chunk mapping and chunk locations in memory; clients ask it only where chunks are, then read and write data directly with chunk servers, so the master is not in the data path. Large chunks keep metadata small and suit sequential batch reads. Copies are placed on at least two racks so a rack switch failure does not lose data. Chunk servers send heartbeats and checksums; when one is missing, the master tells others to copy its chunks until there are 3 copies again. Metadata changes go to a replicated operation log with checkpoints, and a standby master can take over. Batch jobs are scheduled near their data. The trade-off is great throughput for big files versus poor support for many small files.

title: Design a recommendation system at scale
prompt: Design the system that picks "recommended for you" items (videos, products or songs) for 200 million users from a catalog of 50 million items, returning results in under 150 ms and updating soon after users interact.
keyConcepts: Embeddings and approximate nearest neighbor search
thinkAbout: Why do you need a cheap stage that picks a few thousand candidates before a costly ranking stage?
How can embeddings find similar items or users quickly?
Which features does the ranker need at request time, and where do they come from?
How do recent clicks affect results within minutes?
How do you measure success and avoid always showing the same popular items?
outline: Use a multi-stage funnel. Candidate generation pulls a few thousand items from several sources: approximate nearest neighbor search over item embeddings (for example a two-tower model, served by a vector index such as FAISS), "people who liked X also liked Y" lists, trending items and new releases. A ranking service then scores those candidates with a heavier model using user features, item features and context from an online feature store, and a final step re-ranks for diversity, freshness and business rules. Interaction events stream through Kafka to update recent-history features within minutes, while full models retrain daily on logged data in an offline pipeline. Results for very active users can be precomputed and cached. Success is measured with online A/B tests on watch time or purchases, not only offline accuracy. The trade-off is model quality versus latency and compute cost.
